The first three were chosen because each had had its health questioned before and never settled: smoke:share-link carried a cycle-8 OPEN ANOMALY, test:frag was DEAD and revived in cycle 10, test:frag:integration was PERMANENTLY RED and narrowed in cycle 10. guards.exitContractNote: Count-based (not throw-based): `ok()` pushes to `failures`, then `if (failures.length) process.exit(1)`. Every assertion runs on every invocation — all 7 reported in each run below. There is also an early hard exit(1) if the share string is empty, which is correct.
guards.break: Five runs. The first TWO reproduce the cycle-8 anomaly and diagnose it; the last THREE are real falsifications, each applied and reverted independently. (0a) utils/UrlStateEncoder.ts — `key === 'repeats'` added to getDiff's skip-list, the exact cycle-8 break. (0b) same site, `key === 'paramA'` instead, to ask whether `repeats` was special. (0c) `if (1) return ''` at the top of encode(), to prove edits reach the browser at all. (A) same site, `key === 'coloring'` — a whole feature slice absent from the payload, the exact failure mode the cycle-8 `coloring.repeats` assertion was added for. (B) quantize's `parseFloat(obj.toFixed(5))` -> `toFixed(1)`, i.e. encoder precision loss. (C) app-gmt/main.tsx — gated out the `#s=` branch of resolveBootPreset, so the recipient never hydrates from the hash.
guards.result: (0a) GREEN — exit 0, payload 2895 chars, `coloring.repeats round-tripped 3.7 (got 3.7)`. Anomaly reproduced exactly. (0b) GREEN — exit 0, payload byte-identical at 2895, paramA still 0.37. So it was not specific to `repeats`. (0c) RED — exit 1, `getShareString returned a non-empty payload (0 chars)`, proving the module IS on the path and edits DO reach the browser. (A) RED — exit 1, payload 2895 -> 2668, `coloring.repeats round-tripped 3.7 (got 1)`. (B) RED — exit 1, 2 failures: `coreMath.paramA round-tripped 0.37 (got 0.4)`, `materials.roughness round-tripped 0.81 (got 0.8)`. (C) RED — exit 1, 3 failures: paramA got 8, roughness got 0.75, repeats got 2 — the Mandelbulb template's own defaults.
guards.anomalyResolved: SETTLED. The guard was never at fault; the cycle-8 break was a no-op. getDiff's third line (`typeof base !== 'object' ... return current`) returns a subtree VERBATIM when the base side has no counterpart. On the only live path (utils/Sharing.ts -> generateShareStringFromPreset) the base is getFullDefaultPreset(formula), a four-key literal whose `features` is `{}` — so base.features[<anyFeatureId>] is always undefined, every feature slice takes that bail, and recursion STOPS at the feature-id level. A param name in that skip-list is therefore never visited, while a feature id is — which is exactly the (0a)/(0b) GREEN vs (A) RED split. Cycle 8's own leftover probe, debug/_g08c.mts (gitignored, still on disk), shows why it was missed: its fixture base was `{ features: { coloring: { repeats: 1.0, offset: 0 } } }`, i.e. populated, so its recursion behaved nothing like the real one.
guards.fixtureNonDegenerate: Checked per batch-1 lesson 3. Each authored value differs from the value it would hold if the payload dropped it, and break (C) prints that fallback set explicitly: authored 0.37 / 0.81 / 3.7 against template defaults 8 / 0.75 / 2. Break (A) independently shows coloring.repeats falling to 1 (the DDFS param default) when only that slice is dropped. No tautologies.

findings.summary: The cycle-8 OPEN ANOMALY on smoke:share-link is settled: the guard is healthy and the break was a no-op. UrlStateEncoder.getDiff stops recursing at the feature-id level, because the base template it diffs against (getFullDefaultPreset) has `features: {}`, so every feature slice hits the `typeof base !== 'object' -> return current` bail and is copied wholesale. A param name added to the skip-list is never visited; a feature id is. Two corollaries: feature state is not diffed against defaults at all, and the four named skip-list entries (liveModulations, histogramData, interactionSnapshot, *Stack) are unreachable on this path because getPreset never copies them into a Preset.

findings.summary: Nothing in the repo fails when the Fragmentarium importer emits shaders that cannot compile. Gutting the AST renamer in engine-gmt/features/fragmentarium_import/v3/generate/rename.ts — so every imported formula's uniforms keep their original Fragmentarium names and every generated shader references undeclared identifiers — leaves test:frag:integration exit 0 (61 GLSL issues, all classified `warn`) and test:frag exit 0 (60 passed, 0 GLSL issues, because its parse check is syntax-only and unrenamed identifiers are still syntactically valid). Both are cited by .claude/rules/scene-and-formula-format.md for this subsystem.
findings.rationale: Found by falsifying test:frag:integration. The doc side is now fixed (commit 1dc61d24 states plainly what a green run does and does not prove), so no finding rests on a false premise — this is about whether the gate should widen. THE CATCH, and it is why this is not a one-liner: the baseline is not clean. RecFold has carried `Full-shader: Undeclared identifiers: Encountered undefined variable: "OrbitStrength"` since before this sweep, so flipping `warn` to `fail` makes the guard RED ON ARRIVAL — the exact permanently-red state cycle 10 narrowed it out of, and a guard that has never been green cannot distinguish a regression from its baseline. Options: (1) leave it, relying on the corrected header — cheapest and honest, but the hole stays open; (2) gate on `paramIssues` only, whose baseline IS 0 — free today and covers the RENAME_FAIL / DEAD_PARAM / invalid-range categories the file itself calls importer bugs, but it would NOT have caught the renamer break, which produced 0 param issues; (3) gate on GLSL issues against a recorded baseline count of 1, so any NEW parse error fails — catches the renamer break outright, but it is an allowlist, and batch 2's check:zindex finding is precisely about an allowlist exempting the files that mattered; (4) fix RecFold's OrbitStrength gap first, then gate on `glslTotal > 0` with no allowance at all. RECOMMENDATION: (4) if RecFold turns out to be a real importer gap worth closing — it is one formula and it makes the gate honest with no exemption machinery; otherwise (3) with the single baseline entry named and dated in the source. (2) is a poor substitute on its own since it misses the demonstrated break. Not applied: it changes the exit semantics of a guard a rule cites, and which subset to gate is your call.

findings.summary: test:frag's `glslIssues` channel is advisory by design and the baseline is 0, so gating it would be free today — but doing so is a judgement call because the sibling checks inside validateGLSL are heuristics. Prefixing every generated function with a hard GLSL syntax error gives 60 parse errors, 60 passed, 0 failed, exit 0.
findings.rationale: Found while falsifying test:frag. The harness footer already says plainly that glslIssues is 'a warning channel, not a pass/fail signal', so unlike the integration suite this is a stated choice rather than a false claim — nothing was misleading and the doc side needed no correction beyond recording the measurement (done in commit 71d5d4c1). THE CATCH: validateGLSL mixes an objective check with heuristic ones. The parse check is objective — the generated code either parses or it does not. But its siblings hedge in their own wording (`getDist references 'X' which may be out of scope`), and gating a heuristic is how a guard gets weakened later, which is worse than not gating at all. Options: (1) leave it advisory; (2) gate ONLY on issues whose string starts with 'GLSL parse error:', leaving the scope and naming heuristics advisory — narrow, objective, baseline 0, no allowlist needed; (3) gate on everything validateGLSL returns — simplest to read, but adopts the heuristics as contract. RECOMMENDATION: (2). Note it interacts with the test:frag:integration proposal above: the integration suite's full-shader strict parse is strictly stronger than this syntax-only one (it catches undeclared identifiers, which is what the renamer break produced), so if that gate lands, this one is a cheap belt-and-braces rather than the main defence. Not applied: it changes the exit semantics of a guard a rule cites.

findings.summary: test:band-analyser block [5] — the block titled "SuperFlux suppresses a drifting tone, keeps a real onset", covering a mechanism bandAnalyser.ts carries an @invariant about — could not detect that mechanism being removed.
